objective.statement: Write a melody an octave higher or lower, into or out of the alto clef.
successCriteria: I know an octave is eight letter names, seven steps of line and space.
I can move a melody up or down an octave and change its clef.
I can tell this from writing the same pitch in another clef.

explanation.text: Octave transposition means writing music an octave higher or lower than it was. An octave is eight letter names counting both ends, which is seven steps of line and space: a line note becomes a space note and a space note becomes a line note. At Grade 4 you may be asked to do this and change clef at the same time, into or out of the alto clef.

Do not mix this up with the last lesson. Writing the same pitch in another clef keeps the sound exactly the same. Transposing at the octave changes the sound by one octave. The question always says which it wants.

music.textAlternative: A treble stave with three semibreves: E, G and C above middle C.

explanation.caption: The melody in the treble clef.

music.textAlternative: An alto stave with three semibreves: E, G and middle C, one octave lower than the treble melody.

explanation.caption: An octave lower in the alto clef: E3, G3, C4. The new notes are found by name, not by position.

explanation.text: Method: (1) name each note with its octave. (2) Move each name an octave in the direction asked: E4 becomes E3 for an octave lower. (3) Write the new names in the new clef, counting from its anchor. Keep the key signature, because moving an octave does not change the key.
Octave = 8 letter names (7 steps). Name each note, move it an octave, then write it in the new clef. Keep the key signature.

steps: A is on the second line of the alto stave.
An octave higher is seven steps up the stave: the space just above the top line.
Check by counting letters: A B C D E F G A is eight letter names.

provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 7. The alto-clef octave transposition is required at Grade 4 in this course's syllabus mapping although the reference book introduces it in Grade 5 section 3 (p. 107 region); the teaching here is original. Each question includes the alto clef as source or target (treble-to-bass octave transposition is Grade 3 and earns no Grade 4 credit). The question wording always states higher or lower and the target clef.
